And as I came into the cloud of London I met a friend of mine who actually is in a bank, and submitted these suggestions in rhyme to him for use among his colleagues. But he was not very hopeful about the matter. It was not (he assured me) that he underrated the verses, or in any sense lamented their lack of polish. No; it was rather, he felt, an indefinable something in the very atmosphere of the society in which we live that makes it spiritually difficult to sing in banks. And I think he must be right; though the matter is very mysterious. I may observe here that I think there must be some mistake in the calculations of the Socialists. They put down all our distress, not to a moral tone, but to the chaos of private enterprise. Now, banks are private; but post-offices are Socialistic: therefore I naturally expected that the post-office would fall into the collectivist idea of a chorus. Judge of my surprise when the lady in my local post-office (whom I urged to sing) dismissed the idea with far more coldness than the bank clerk had done. She seemed indeed, to be in a considerably greater state of depression than he. Should any one suppose that this was the effect of the verses themselves, it is only fair to say that the specimen verse of the Post-Office Hymn ran thus:

“O’er London our letters are shaken like snow, Our wires o’er the world like the thunderbolts go. The news that may marry a maiden in Sark, Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”

Chorus (with a swing of joy and energy):

“Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”

And the more I thought about the matter the more painfully certain it seemed that the most important and typical modern things could not be done with a chorus. One could not, for instance, be a great financier and sing; because the essence of being a great financier is that you keep quiet. You could not even in many modern circles be a public man and sing; because in those circles the essence of being a public man is that you do nearly everything in private. Nobody would imagine a chorus of money-lenders. Every one knows the story of the solicitors’ corps of volunteers who, when the Colonel on the battlefield cried “Charge!” all said simultaneously, “Six-and-eightpence.” Men can sing while charging in a military, but hardly in a legal sense. And at the end of my reflections I had really got no further than the sub-conscious feeling of my friend the bank-clerk—that there is something spiritually suffocating about our life; not about our laws merely, but about our life. Bank-clerks are without songs, not because they are poor, but because they are sad. Sailors are much poorer. As I passed homewards I passed a little tin building of some religious sort, which was shaken with shouting as a trumpet is torn with its own tongue. THEY were singing anyhow; and I had for an instant a fancy I had often had before: that with us the super-human is the only place where you can find the human. Human nature is hunted and has fled into sanctuary.

message.content:
As I entered the fog of London, I encountered a friend who works at a bank. I shared with him my poetic proposals intended for his coworkers. However, he expressed a lack of optimism regarding the potential reception of my verses. He assured me that it wasn't that he undervalued the poetry or regretted its lack of refinement. Rather, he sensed an elusive quality inherent in our societal atmosphere that makes it spiritually challenging to express oneself musically within banks. I found his perspective compelling, albeit somewhat enigmatic. Additionally, I believe the Socialists have miscalculated certain aspects of our distress. They attribute our struggles not to a moral failing but to the disorder of private enterprise. Given that banks operate privately while post-offices embody a more socialistic approach, I had anticipated that the post-office might readily embrace my idea of a collective song. Imagine my astonishment when the clerk at my local post-office, whom I encouraged to sing, responded with a chill far greater than that of the bank employee. In fact, her demeanor seemed even more disheartened.

If one were to think that my verses prompted her lack of enthusiasm, it's important to clarify that the sample line from the Post-Office Hymn was quite spirited: “O’er London our letters are shaken like snow, Our wires o’er the world like the thunderbolts go. The news that may marry a maiden in Sark, Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.” The jubilant chorus, “Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park,” was meant to evoke joy and energy. Yet, the more I contemplated the situation, the more it became painfully evident that the most significant aspects of contemporary life resist being encapsulated in song. For instance, one cannot be a successful financier while also singing, as the core of financial success lies in maintaining silence. Similarly, in many modern environments, being a public figure often entails conducting one's affairs privately. The concept of a chorus composed of money-lenders is almost laughable; people are familiar with the anecdote about volunteer solicitors on the battlefield, who, when commanded to “Charge!” collectively responded with “Six-and-eightpence.” While men may sing during a military charge, such expressions are unlikely in legal contexts.

Ultimately, my reflections led me back to the instinctive realization shared by my bank-clerk friend—that our existence often feels spiritually stifling. This isn’t merely about our laws; it encompasses the essence of our daily lives. Bank clerks may lack songs not due to poverty, but rather because of a deeper sadness. In stark contrast, sailors, who experience greater financial hardship, often carry a different spirit. On my way home, I passed a small tin structure associated with a religious group, which resonated with the sound of exuberant singing, akin to a trumpet bursting forth with its own voice. In that moment, I was struck by a recurring thought: in our society, the divine seems to be the only realm where genuine humanity can be found. It feels as though human nature is pursued relentlessly, ultimately seeking refuge in the sacred.
